title: How to check if silver jewellery is real at home
description: Six simple home tests to check if your silver jewellery is real, what each test can and cannot prove, and when to take a piece to a jeweller instead.
keywords: how to check real silver at home
how to identify real silver jewellery
intro: You can get a good idea of whether silver jewellery is real at home using a magnet, an ice cube, a white cloth and a close look at the stamp. None of these tests is perfect on its own, but when three or four point the same way, you can be fairly confident. For certainty, a jeweller's test is the final word.

sections.heading: Test 1: Read the stamp properly
paragraphs: Start with the easiest check. Use your phone camera on zoom and look at the clasp, the back of the pendant, the bail or the inside of a ring. Real sterling is usually marked 925, S925, Sterling or Ster. Fine silver may be marked 999. Some pieces also carry a hallmark with additional symbols.

A missing stamp does not always mean fake, especially on small, old or handmade pieces. A stamp is also not proof on its own, because it can be pressed into any metal. Treat it as a first clue, and if the stamp is unclear, ask the seller what purity they are selling and whether the piece is hallmarked.

sections.heading: Test 2: The magnet test
paragraphs: Silver is not magnetic. Hold a strong magnet, like a fridge magnet or one from an old speaker, close to the piece. If the jewellery jumps towards it or sticks, it has iron or steel inside and is not solid silver.

If nothing happens, that is a good sign but not proof. Brass, copper, aluminium and many alloys are not magnetic either. Note also that the clasp spring may contain steel, so test the main body of the piece.

sections.heading: Test 3: The ice cube test
paragraphs: Silver conducts heat extremely well. Place an ice cube on a flat silver surface, such as the back of a pendant or a silver coin, and another on a steel spoon or plastic surface for comparison. On real silver, the ice starts melting noticeably faster, as if the metal is pulling heat into it.
This works best on flat, heavier items. A thin chain does not have enough surface for a clear result.

sections.heading: Test 4: The white cloth rub
paragraphs: Take a soft white cotton cloth and rub a small area of the piece firmly. If dark grey or black marks appear on the cloth, the metal has been oxidising, and that is typical of real silver. Silver tarnish comes off onto the cloth.

No mark is not necessarily bad news: a freshly polished or rhodium-plated piece may leave the cloth clean. But if you see yellow or greenish marks, there may be brass or copper showing through a coating.

sections.heading: Test 5: Look, listen and smell
paragraphs: These are softer checks, useful only alongside the others.
list: Look at worn edges, the inside of the clasp and the back of the bail. A different colour peeking through, especially yellowish or reddish, points to plating.
Gently tap two silver coins or a silver piece against a coin. Silver tends to give a clear, ringing tone, while many base metals sound duller. This needs a practised ear.
Hold the piece in a warm hand for a minute, then smell it. A strong metallic, coin-like smell often comes from copper or brass. Sterling has very little smell.

sections.heading: Tests you should skip at home
paragraphs: You will find videos suggesting bleach, nitric acid or scratching the piece against a tile. Avoid these. Bleach will blacken real silver quickly and can damage stones and plating. Acid testing kits exist, but they require a scratch on the piece, careful handling of corrosive liquid and some experience reading the colours. Scratching a piece to see what is under it damages the very thing you are trying to check.
If the home tests leave you unsure, take the piece to a jeweller who can do an acid test properly or use an XRF machine, which reads the metal content without harming the jewellery.

sections.heading: Buying smart so you test less
paragraphs: The easiest way to avoid a fake is to buy where the purity is clearly written and returns are possible. faq.q: Does real silver stick to a magnet?
faq.a: No. Silver is not magnetic. If a piece sticks to a magnet, it contains iron or steel, though a non-magnetic piece is not automatically silver.

faq.q: Can fake silver have a 925 stamp?
faq.a: Yes. A stamp can be pressed into any metal, so use it as one clue along with the other tests and the seller's reputation.

faq.q: Does real silver leave a black mark on cloth?
faq.a: Often yes. Tarnished silver leaves grey or black marks when rubbed with a white cloth. Freshly polished or rhodium-plated pieces may not.

faq.q: What is the most accurate way to test silver?
faq.a: An XRF test at a jeweller or testing centre. It reads metal content without damaging the piece.
